newsitem.title: USA: Regulations seen hindering Asia air cargo service.
newsitem.headline: Regulations seen hindering Asia air cargo service.

text.p: Regulatory hurdles in Asia restrict cargo carriers from transporting goods between two foreign nations, inflate prices and limit service, air cargo executives said.

"Protectionist aviation regimes curtail competition, growth and innovation, while denying consumers and communities the opportunity for better and more frequent service, lower pricing and improved quality," Bruce Barash, a regional vice president for MSAS Cargo International, said at the Sixth Annual Phoenix International Aviation Symposium.
MSAS is part of London-based Ocean Group Plc.

Regulatory policies in some Asian nations require cargo companies to submit to lengthy customs procedures and local laws requiring the use of local crews to load and unload planes. These policies delay shipments and add costs, said Mark Allen, a vice president of the Asia Pacific division at Federal Express Corp.

"We cannot satisfy the universal need for speed if, due to restrictive, anti-competitive government policies, we are denied the right to load and off-load our own aircraft, clear cargo quickly through customers or pick-up and delivery traffic at our customers' facilities," Allen said.
"We should not be required to use the services of a third-party monopoly operator... who is not likley to share our sense of purpose or urgency," Allen said.
The Asian-Pacific market is fastest growing air traffic market in the world. The Asian market is expected to increase from 42 percent of the worldwide market to 50 percent by 2013, Allen said.
Cargo carriers will not be able to keep up with this growth unless more liberal "open skies" aviation treaties are formed with Asian nations, air cargo executives said.

"The campaign to liberalize world air transport for a global open skies policy .... would obviously be a superior alternative to the existing regulatory status of narrow bilateral treaties and mini-deals which governs the air transport industry today," Barash said.

But executives stressed that air cargo agreements must be structured independently of passenger agreements. Cargo companies must be allowed to add or eliminate service points, change aircraft and transport goods freely according to market demands, not regulatory requirements.

"The U.S. government must consistently recognize that air cargo agreements entered into with other countries in the Asia-Pacific region cannot be made as corollaries to those which address passenger service concerns," Allen said.

"Transportations should be treated as trade, not regulation. Airlines should be freed of regulatory constraints so they can focus on transporting customers and goods," said Robert Frenzel, vice president of United Parcel Service of America Inc.
